The Convention for the Protection of the Architectural Heritage of Europe (), also referred to as the Granada Convention (), is a legally binding instrument that sets the framework for an effective conservation approach within Europe. Out of the forty-three member states of the Council of Europe, forty-two have ratified or acceded to the convention since it was opened for signature in 1985, and it entered into force on 1 December 1987.
After 30 years of collaboration among member states of the Council of Europe, this convention constitutes an important framework for the safeguarding of the cultural heritage of monuments and sites.
The Convention for the Protection of the Architectural Heritage in Europe, along with the Framework Convention on the Value of Cultural Heritage for Society, the Faro Convention, and the European Convention on the Protection of the Archaeological Heritage, comprise the thrust of cultural heritage protection and development in Europe.
Issues under the convention
The issues addressed in this convention are defined by the following objectives:
* Support the idea of solidarity and cooperation among European parties, in relation to heritage conservation.
* Include principles of "conservation policies" within the framework of European cooperation.
* Strengthen and promote policies for the conservation and development of cultural heritage in Europe.
About the convention
As mentioned in the preamble, the starting point of this convention was the European Cultural Convention signed in 1954. After that, the first action toward the protection of cultural heritage, promoted by the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, began in 1963 with the creation of Europa Nostra, which promoted the intergovernmental cooperation within Europe.
Structure
Preamble
The overall aim is first, to provide cultural references that improve their environment in the European context, and second to foster a sustainable development taking into consideration economic growth and social development. It is stated that European parties, through the adoption of common principles, can commit themselves in a permanent collaboration on conservation policies. This can be seen by the accordance of minimum safeguard agreements regarding architectural heritage. It is mentioned that in matters of cultural and built heritage, the Council of Europe has been working over 30 years. It expresses the purpose and the European philosophy regarding conservation issues.
Definition of the architectural heritage
It contains the three definitions of heritage defined by the 1972 UNESCO Convention for the Protection of the World Cultural and Natural Heritage. This comprises the description of monuments, groups of buildings and sites.
Identification of properties to be protected
This section is set out in Article 2, which establishes the conduct of a survey through the creation of an inventory. This will permit not only the documentation of heritage, as defined in Article 1, but also the assessment of properties as the initial step towards legal protection.
Statutory protection procedures
This part is defined by Articles 3, 4, and 5. It contains the legal, political, and administrative measures to be taken by each Party for protecting the properties in question. These measures will be applied differently in each region or state. It also describes in Article 4, the legal actions applicable to the protected heritage, that ensure the supervision of work affecting protected properties.
Ancillary measures
Composed of Articles 6, 7, and 8, this section explains the types of financial support that public authorities may give to guarantee, facilitate, and encourage the maintenance and restoration of protected properties. It also mentions the various measures to consider regarding the environment, such as public spaces and pollution control.
Sanctions
It contains only Article 9, which explains Parties may ensure that infringements of the laws protecting heritage receive an adequate response through criminal or administrative law.
Conservation policies
This section consists of Articles 10, 11, 12 and 13. It describes principles of integrated conservation of heritage, as reflected in the previous work of the Council of Europe. It also explains the principle of maintenance through the use of heritage, previously described in Article 5 of the Venice Charter, ICOMOS.Venice Charter
ICOMOS It also states that there must be balance between use and conservation, which will conserve the architectural and historical value of the property. This goal is supported by the principles of integrated conservation explained in Article 13, which implies an effective cooperation between the administrative departments concerned.
Participation and associations
It contains Article 14, and describes the establishment of structures to facilitate cooperation between Parties or concerned regions.
Information and training
It contains Articles 15 and 16 and explains the importance of public participation at an early stage, as a whole to appreciate and understand heritage. This might concern training systems and trades involved in conservation.
European co-ordination of conservation policies
Defined by Articles 17, 18, 19, 20 and 21. Articles 17 and 18 contain the description of the coordination of European conservation policies. They also describe the technical assistance system under Council of Europe. Article 19 highlights the importance of exchanges and trade among the heritage conservation professionals. Article 20 recommends the creation of a monitoring committee to ensure the successful application of the convention.
Final clauses
This section consists of Articles 22, 23, 24,25, 26 and 27, which contains the Europe Council's final clauses for conventions and agreements.
Ratification
As of January 2025, Forty-two states have ratified the convention, either by signing, acceding to it, or succeeding to it. They are as follows:
